subject: Cognitive Science
title: The Sunk Cost Fallacy
description: A quick, practical guide to The Sunk Cost Fallacy.

hook.text: You've watched 90 minutes of a terrible film. You stay because you've 'already invested the time.'

buildup.text: The sunk cost fallacy: past investments—time, money, effort—shouldn't affect future decisions, but they do.

discovery.text: Rationally, only future costs and benefits matter. The money already spent is gone regardless.

twist.text: Businesses sink billions into failing projects because leaders won't abandon their prior commitments.

climax.text: The Concorde jet was continued for decades despite guaranteed losses—now economists call it the Concorde fallacy.

punchline.text: What you've spent shouldn't decide what you do next.

quiz.question: What is the sunk cost fallacy?
options: Letting past investment drive future decisions

details.summary: The sunk cost fallacy is continuing an action because of past investment rather than future returns. People stay at a bad movie because they paid for tickets, or continue a failing project because of money already spent. Rational choice should only consider future costs and benefits.
details.whyItMatters: Sunk cost thinking traps people in bad decisions. It wastes resources in business, relationships, and public policy by honoring past investment over future value.
takeaways: Past costs should not influence forward-looking decisions
People honor investments even when continuing is wasteful
Organizations are especially vulnerable to sunk cost escalation

faq.question: Why is the sunk cost fallacy so hard to overcome?
faq.answer: Abandoning an investment feels like admitting failure, triggering loss aversion. People also feel responsible for creating the waste. Social pressure adds another layer: changing course is seen as inconsistency or weakness. These emotional forces make it harder to cut losses rationally.

faq.question: How can you avoid the sunk cost fallacy?
faq.answer: Ask: if I were starting fresh with no prior investment, would I make this same choice? Reframe the decision in terms of future costs and benefits only. Establish predetermined exit criteria before starting a project so that stopping is a planned response, not a felt failure.
